prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean, quantitative case of a new measurement regime opened by a basic quantum idea: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be interrogated with the light shift cancelled, and Ye's work took the many-atom clock to 10^-18 and below, with controlled many-body effects. The result has been verified and compared across many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), it is metrologically unambiguous, and it already enables relativistic geodesy at millimetre scales and bounds on variation of constants and dark matter. Eight of eight members ranked it, which is unusual breadth, but I rest my support on the physics: the discovery is the technique and the regime it opens, it builds on rather than repeats the 2005 frequency-comb prize, and the two-person attribution is about as clean as a modern experimental prize gets. I have moved it above my own opening first choice, circuit QED, because on reflection I cannot make the case for cQED without the timing and overlap problems I raised myself.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is attribution at the edges: Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and the ion-clock community (Wineland-type approaches) all made real contributions, and Ye's own wider body of work (combs, ultracold molecules, thorium-229) could blur the citation. There is also a legitimate question, raised by Olsson, of whether another precision-spectroscopy prize so soon after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control is the most valuable use of a slot. The pending redefinition of the SI second is not a scientific criterion, but a committee may feel the technology story has not yet culminated. None of this seems to me to defeat the case, but it is why the citation should name the lattice clock specifically.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because it is the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed, fits the 2005 comb and 1989/2012 precision-spectroscopy tradition, and gives a clean two-person prize, while admitting he cannot verify every priority claim from memory.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific reading and with the two-name configuration. On priority I can add some support from my own side of the field: the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration are Katori's, while the push to the lowest systematic uncertainty, long coherence and Fermi-degenerate operation is Ye's, so the credit splits along a distinction that is easy to state in a citation. I would, however, push back gently on 'tradition' as an argument. The prior prizes show the committee values precision spectroscopy, not that this one qualifies. It qualifies because the lattice clock opened a regime, many-atom interrogation at 10^-18 with controlled interactions, that single-ion approaches do not reach.

responses.point: Olsson ranks lattice clocks fourth, finds the two-person list defensible, but notes that the 2005 prize already recognised Hall and Hansch for the frequency comb which Ye used, that other lattice-clock groups are not credited, and that the redefinition of the second is pending.
responses.response: The comb overlap is fair to raise, but I think it argues for careful wording rather than against the candidate. The comb is the enabling ruler that reads out the optical frequency. The lattice clock is a different discovery, namely the choice of the magic wavelength and the many-atom interrogation scheme that give both accuracy and stability. That is the same relation as between the 2001 BEC prize and later cold-atom work. I agree the other groups matter, but on every list I have seen Katori and Ye are the principal originators, and the independent confirmations (PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) are what make the discovery mature, not competing priority claims. I also agree with you that the pending redefinition of the second is not a reason to wait.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clean model meeting experiment, with a simple general mechanism and large downstream impact, and ranks optical lattice clocks only eighth though acknowledging them as mature.
responses.response: I take the simple-mechanism-with-large-impact argument seriously, and twisted bilayer graphene does have that character. My qualification is about interpretation and credit rather than importance. The superconducting pairing and the correlated insulators are still debated, and the credit is entangled with Cao's first-author role, the Dean and Young groups and the earlier Lopes dos Santos et al. theory, as you note yourself. The lattice clock has the opposite profile: the underlying quantum mechanics is settled, the result is verified quantitatively by several institutes, and the credit is two names. I would not exclude B024, since I defer to you and Eriksson on materials, but I think it is the stronger candidate in a few years, when the pairing question is clearer, rather than now.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as the clearest discovery that nature delivered and never recognised on the experimental side, while accepting that attribution among founders and leaders of ATLAS and CMS is imperfect.
responses.response: I agree the Higgs observation is the most important single result among these candidates, and that is not what is in dispute. My difficulty is the one you and Mehlig both name: a prize needs credited persons whose contributions can be tied to the discovery, and the three names proposed are founders and project leaders, not obviously those who made the 2012 measurement. Unless we can settle that attribution convincingly, for example by a different citation or different people, I think B010 is a harder prize to award fairly than the lattice clock, even though it is a larger discovery. I would keep it off my own configuration but would not argue against others who find a defensible attribution.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first and the lattice clock third, valuing instrumentation plus discovery, and notes that the credited pair omits the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers while the diffuse flux is stable and timely.
responses.response: I share your respect for IceCube and for results that nature hands us through a new instrument, and the Halzen and Spiering attribution is indeed cleaner than most. Where I am more cautious is maturity: the diffuse flux is solid, but the source identifications rest on few objects and I defer to you and Danielsson on how mature the community regards them. I would place B043 as a strong later candidate. I also note that you rank the lattice clock third with the same names I propose, so I think the committee already has a common reading on attribution for B052, and our remaining differences are about priority between very different fields.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the citation to name the lattice clock specifically or to use broader wording about precision measurement, given the contributions of other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups.

Whether circuit QED (B056) should be treated as a distinct discovery from the 2025 recognition of macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and whether the Blais omission can be resolved with three names; I regard this as open and I am not the right member to settle it.
How much weight to give the pending redefinition of the SI second; I regard it as irrelevant to merit but others may not.
Fair attribution for B010 and B024, which are outside my expertise and where I defer to colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a Chalmers MC2 theorist working on superconducting circuits, so I have a close professional connection to the field of B056 (circuit QED) and to groups around it, and I would recuse myself from the final decision on B056 if it became a live option. I also co-authored the observation of the dynamical Casimir effect with colleagues at Chalmers. For B052 (Katori and Ye) and the other shortlisted candidates, no specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
